title: HarborEdge Logistics - Private VPC Discovery
summary: Discovery call focused on HarborEdge's requirements for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood. Key concerns were network connectivity options (VPC peering vs private endpoints vs transit gateway), cross-account routing, egress controls and auditability, KMS integration, and region/data residency. Next steps: share security pack, connectivity diagrams, pricing estimate for Dedicated vs Private, propose pilot steps and schedule a network workshop.
next_steps: Redwood to share security documentation and SOC2 report (Sophie)
Schedule a 1-hour network workshop to map VPC/topology (Daniel + Aisha)
Provide pricing estimate for Private deployment and dedicated pool options (Sophie)
Customer to provide current VPC CIDR ranges and preferred region (Tom)
Send example connectivity diagram and recommended NAT/egress pattern (Daniel)
action_items: Sophie Martinez: Send security packet + SOC2 + compliance matrix; due 2026-04-02
Daniel Cho: Prepare connectivity diagram and sample CloudFormation for VPC endpoints and peering; due 2026-04-06
Tom Reynolds: Share current VPC CIDRs, account IDs, and preferred AWS region; due 2026-04-03
transcript:
[00:00] Sophie Martinez: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sophie, account exec at Redwood. We got Daniel from the SE team on as well. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Tom Reynolds: Doing well, thanks. Busy week but excited to get into this.
[00:11] Aisha Khan: Hi, yes. Aisha here, lead infra. We want to understand options for running Redwood in our private AWS environment — networking, security, the whole thing.
[00:18] Daniel Cho: Great. We'll start high-level then dive into network topology. Quick ask: what's your primary goal — latency, data residency, or isolation for compliance?
[00:26] Luis Ortega: Security and compliance first. We're regulated so keys and logs have to remain under our control. Latency matters for our routing engine but less than meeting compliance.
[00:34] Sophie Martinez: Perfect. So Redwood offers hosted, dedicated, and private. Sounds like Private is the target — we can run the control plane managed or customer-managed depending on your needs. We'll focus on Private VPC patterns.
[00:45] Tom Reynolds: Yeah Private. We heard about VPC peering and private endpoints. Also curious about cross-account setup because we separate infra and security accounts.
[00:52] Daniel Cho: Totally. There are three common architectures: 1) VPC peering cross-account directly between your VPCs and the Redwood VPC; 2) AWS PrivateLink / interface VPC endpoints exposed into your VPC; or 3) transit gateway connecting multiple VPCs into a shared services VPC. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:06] Aisha Khan: Could you expand on tradeoffs? We have overlapping CIDRs sometimes and a shared security account that owns KMS.
[01:13] Daniel Cho: Sure. VPC peering is simple and low-latency but doesn't support transitive routing — meaning you'd need peering per pair of VPCs. Also overlapping CIDRs block peering. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) avoids peering and is cross-account friendly, and you keep control of your subnets and route tables. Transit gateway supports many VPCs and simplifies central routing but adds cost and an extra network hop.
[01:28] Luis Ortega: For KMS, we need keys in our security account and some HSM-backed keys — can Redwood integrate with our KMS?
[01:34] Sophie Martinez: Yes, integration with customer-managed KMS is supported in Private deployments. For HSM-backed keys we work with the KMS customer key policies; we can sign agreements and provide key access patterns used by the runtime. We'll share our KMS integration guide.
[01:47] Tom Reynolds: And what about private endpoints for the inference service itself — do we put an ENI in our subnet?
[01:52] Daniel Cho: With PrivateLink we provision interface endpoints in your subnet — those ENIs are managed in your account. Traffic never goes over the public internet. It's common for customers who want strict egress policies.
[02:03] Aisha Khan: That sounds like what we want. How do you handle egress to other AWS services, like fetching models from S3 or telemetry?
[02:11] Daniel Cho: Two parts: model artifacts and telemetry. For model artifacts we can either pull from your S3 via VPC endpoint (gateway endpoint) or you can pre-stage models in the Redwood-controlled S3 if you prefer. Telemetry and metrics can be routed to your monitoring stack via VPC peering or a private collector endpoint; alternatively, Redwood can push to a customer-provided forwarder over the private link. We'll work with whatever your security team prefers.
[02:31] Luis Ortega: Do you support keeping audit logs in our account?
[02:34] Sophie Martinez: Yes — audit logging can be delivered to your S3 or your SIEM via syslog/forwarder in your VPC. We also retain internal operational logs for debugging but we can restrict retention and provide an audit trail.
[02:45] Tom Reynolds: Region question — we want deployment in us-east-1 for low latency to our fleet, but we also have some EU data residency constraints. Can Redwood support multi-region private deployments?
[02:54] Daniel Cho: Absolutely. We can deploy Private stacks into specific regions. You can pin model serving hosts to a region. For cross-region traffic you can replicate models to each region's storage or use cross-region S3 replication. Cost and latency effects vary.
[03:07] Aisha Khan: If we do multi-region, how does routing and failover work? We need graceful degradation if us-east-1 has issues.
[03:14] Daniel Cho: We recommend a primary/secondary routing policy: route by region with health checks. If the primary region fails, we trigger failover to the secondary. For model consistency we can version pin to avoid drift, and pre-warm the secondary with model cache to meet latency SLOs.
[03:26] Tom Reynolds: What's the latency impact of pre-warming vs on-demand?
[03:29] Daniel Cho: Pre-warming keeps KV caches and warmed GPU contexts so first token latency is similar to steady-state. On-demand cold starts can add seconds depending on model size. We'll provide guidance based on your model families.
[03:39] Luis Ortega: Okay, let's talk network specifics. We have a security account that owns our central NAT and transit gateway. We don't want outbound internet for model downloads — everything must go via our NAT with logging.
[03:50] Daniel Cho: That's common. You can force egress through your NAT in the shared services VPC, and we can ensure the Redwood host subnets use your route table. If using PrivateLink, calls to the Redwood endpoints are inside your VPC; any outbound that the Redwood runtime needs (e.g., to fetch models) can be routed through your NAT by default. We can also ship model artifacts via your S3 behind VPC endpoints so no public egress is needed.
[04:07] Aisha Khan: How about cross-account role assumption? Do you require any IAM roles in our account for provisioning?
[04:12] Sophie Martinez: For Private deployments we typically use CloudFormation or Terraform templates that require a deploy role with limited permissions. We can run a remote deploy model or hand you templates to run in your account. For operations we use IAM roles with least privilege and vendor-specific policies. We can also support an agentless model where you run everything but that increases operational load on your side.
[04:30] Tom Reynolds: We prefer templates we can review. We won't hand over full account access.
[04:34] Daniel Cho: Totally understood. We'll provide a template and a narrow deploy role.
[04:39] Luis Ortega: For network CIDRs, what do you need from us?
[04:42] Daniel Cho: We'll need the VPC CIDRs, the subnets where you want interface endpoints or hosts, and any restricted routing or firewall rules. If you have overlapping CIDRs we can use PrivateLink instead of peering.
[04:53] Aisha Khan: We have multiple subnets across AZs and we care about high-availability across AZs.
[04:58] Daniel Cho: The Redwood Private stack supports multi-AZ; we recommend at least two AZs for high availability. We'll provision ENIs or hosts across AZs.
[05:06] Tom Reynolds: Anything special for Kubernetes-based infra? We're running EKS for most services.
[05:10] Daniel Cho: If you're running EKS and want to keep the runtime within Kubernetes, we have an operator pattern and also a VM-based runtime. For strict isolation and GPU access we often recommend dedicated GPU hosts outside of EKS, but both models are supported. Daniel to follow up with more specifics.
[05:24] Sophie Martinez: On the compliance front, Luis, you mentioned HSM-backed KMS. What are your audit requirements (retention, log forwarding)?
[05:31] Luis Ortega: Logs need to be retained for seven years for some workloads. We also need CloudTrail style events, request-level logs for inference requests going to our SIEM. Also SSO via our IdP (Okta).
[05:41] Daniel Cho: We can deliver request-level logs to your S3 and CloudWatch in your account and also integrate with Okta via SAML/SCIM for user management. We'll provide the mapping for RBAC.
[05:50] Aisha Khan: Can we do VPC endpoints for both control plane and data plane?
[05:54] Daniel Cho: Yes. Many customers expose the control plane endpoints through PrivateLink and the data plane (inference endpoints) via either PrivateLink or by hosting the runtime directly in their VPC. If the runtime is hosted in your VPC, network egress control is straightforward since everything is your VPC.
[06:09] Tom Reynolds: Cost implications? We want to understand the delta between Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity vs running Private in our account.
[06:16] Sophie Martinez: Good question. Dedicated reserves capacity in our environment for your team — you get predictable throughput and Redwood manages the infra, but data crosses Redwood-managed networks (with contractual controls). Private means you pay for the customer infra (EC2/GPU, NAT, transit) as well as Redwood's platform fee. Private can be more expensive in raw infra cost but gives you stronger isolation and compliance posture. We'll prepare a side-by-side estimate.
[06:37] Luis Ortega: We need to present cost to finance — include expected egress, NAT, and endpoint costs.
[06:42] Sophie Martinez: We'll include the detailed cost components.
[06:45] Aisha Khan: Operational runbook — in the event of an incident, what's your support model?
[06:49] Sophie Martinez: For Private we offer playbooks, 24/7 support for enterprise tiers, and runbooks we co-own. For critical incidents we can open a war room and we have on-call SEs. We'll include escalation paths.
[06:59] Tom Reynolds: One more — can we run in a closed air-gapped environment?
[07:03] Daniel Cho: For extremely locked-down customers we offer an on-prem Private package. That usually requires an engagement to validate hardware and network. It's more of a multi-week project but feasible.
[07:12] Luis Ortega: Good to know. For now we want Private in AWS.
[07:15] Sophie Martinez: Next up, let's capture some specific artifacts we'll need. Aisha, can you list the pieces we'll share?
[07:21] Aisha Khan: Sure — current VPC CIDRs, account IDs, preferred region (us-east-1), list of subnets and AZs, and our KMS ARNs. Also our security questionnaire which we've attached.
[07:31] Sophie Martinez: Great. We'll send a short checklist and the security pack. Daniel will prepare a connectivity diagram showing PrivateLink and transit gateway options.
[07:39] Daniel Cho: I'll also include a CloudFormation example for the interface endpoint, the security group rules we recommend, and a sample route table layout.
[07:48] Tom Reynolds: On timing, we want a pilot in Q2 if possible. We're aiming for a POC where we run a subset of traffic through Redwood Private.
[07:56] Sophie Martinez: That timeline sounds achievable. For a pilot we'd typically scope a small dedicated pool (or private stack) for a single model family and a limited set of routes.
[08:06] Aisha Khan: Do you have limits on number of requests per second per host? We have spikes up to a few hundred rps during batch windows.
[08:12] Daniel Cho: Per-host throughput depends on model size and GPU. We can map expected throughput per GPU type; for spikes we recommend autoscaling and some burst capacity. We'll include throughput profiles in the follow-up.
[08:24] Luis Ortega: Security questionnaire — you said you'd provide a filled-out template?
[08:27] Sophie Martinez: We'll provide a completed questionnaire and the SOC2 report plus the compliance matrix showing how Redwood maps to your controls.
[08:36] Tom Reynolds: Any changes to our identity that's needed? We use Okta and SCIM.
[08:40] Daniel Cho: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. For admin access we recommend SAML with group-to-role mapping. We'll include a sample SAML metadata doc.
[08:50] Aisha Khan: Networking nuance — if we go with PrivateLink, do you support endpoint services across accounts with acceptance flows?
[08:56] Daniel Cho: Yes. We'll publish an endpoint service and your account will accept. We'll need the account ID(s) and subnet IDs where the endpoints will be created. There's an acceptance step which your admins perform.
[09:07] Tom Reynolds: Are there any limits on endpoints per region we should be aware of?
[09:11] Daniel Cho: AWS has ENI limits per instance and per subnet, so we recommend dedicated subnets for endpoints and ensure your quotas are sufficient. We'll document recommended subnet sizes.
[09:21] Luis Ortega: For monitoring, what telemetry do you collect and how granular is request data?
[09:26] Daniel Cho: We collect anonymized performance metrics by default. For Private we can capture request-level metadata (headers, latency, token counts) and deliver to your SIEM. We avoid storing PII by default unless required; we can work through retention and redaction rules.
[09:42] Sophie Martinez: Quick check — any blockers we haven't covered?
[09:45] Aisha Khan: Overlap CIDRs might push us away from peering. We'll check and send ranges.
[09:50] Tom Reynolds: Also need the cost delta.
[09:52] Sophie Martinez: We'll deliver cost delta in the follow-up.
[09:55] Daniel Cho: I'll call out recommended route tables, NAT pattern, and PrivateLink vs transit gateway pros/cons in the network workshop.
[10:03] Aisha Khan: Do you have a recommended pattern for egress logging? We want connection logs and request-level logs to flow to our Splunk.
[10:09] Daniel Cho: Use VPC Flow Logs plus our request-level log forwarder to push JSON lines to your S3 or a Kinesis/Firehose into Splunk. We'll include a sample pipeline.
[10:19] Tom Reynolds: Anything on certificate management for intra-VPC TLS?
[10:23] Daniel Cho: We use mTLS between internal services. For customer-facing endpoints we can integrate with ACM or bring-your-own certs. For internal, we can exchange certs during provisioning or use your internal PKI.
[10:35] Sophie Martinez: Alright looks like good coverage. We'll recap action items and next steps.
[10:40] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good.
[10:42] Sophie Martinez: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the security pack and schedule the network workshop for next week.
[10:48] Aisha Khan: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:50] Luis Ortega: Thanks all.
[10:52] END TRANSCRIPT
